newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ power station to find new life in rubbish.
newsitem.headline: NZ power station to find new life in rubbish.

text.p: The mothballed Meremere power station came a step closer to finding a new lease of life in rubbish incineration on Friday with the announcement by Electricity Corporation of New Zealand that negotiations for its sale had reached an advanced stage.
Olivine New Zealand Ltd plans to buy the station and convert it into a rubbish incinerator to produce electricity which could be sold either to the national grid or directly to individual users.
Meremere is a coal fired 180 megawatt station mothballed by ECNZ in 1991.

"Meremere is a staged process. The first stage is to recommission the coal plant, the second stage is the implementation, the construction of and phasing in of rubbish to be burnt in the high temperature kilns and incinerators," Olivine director Tony Huston said.

Huston said resource consent applications had been lodged with the Waikato regional and district councils. He said the project had considerable benefits, not the least of which was the elimination of landfills.

"Landfills are nothing other than a timebomb really," Huston said. "You've got these huge depressions into the ground which become mountains, dangerous gases coming out of them and all this sort of nonsense...and we've now got the technology to cleanly destroy the stuff and to get a beneficial product at the end."
Olivine was a wholly-owned New Zealand company but was related to Olivine in the United States, which makes incinerators. "We've got the rights to the (Olivine) technology," Huston said.

"There's a lot of opportunity. We've got a lot of enquiries from overseas to go on and do the same sort of thing (elsewhere in New Zealand). The interesting aspect of it is...we are utilising the old, existing infrastructure and breathing new life into it. The key to it is to bring this very old plant into the 90s by automation."

To his knowledge, it would be the first waste-burning operation to produce electricity in New Zealand. "We'll start with probably 30 megawatts and build it up to 60 and then 120," Huston said. -- Wellington newsroom (64 4) 473 4746
